newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Payrolls, payrolls, payrolls.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Payrolls, payrolls, payrolls.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market faces what could be a watershed on Friday -- the release of the February U.S. employment report.

In a Reuters poll, economists estimated, on average, that payrolls expanded by 230,000 jobs in February after growing by 271,000 jobs in Janaury. The unemployment rate dropped to 5.3 percent from January's 5.4 percent level, they estimated. Average hourly earnings likely rose by 0.4 perent in February while the average workweek lengthened to 34.6 hours from 34.1 hours, the economists said.

"There's a lot riding on the employment report, more than normal," said Dana Johnson, managing director and head of research at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc. "There's a sense that the nature of that report might determine whether the Federal Reserve tightens monetary policy in March."
An employment report that is strong in all its aspects could persuade the Federal Reserve to tighten interest rates at its policy meeting on March 25, some Fed watchers believe.

On the other hand, an employment report in which payrolls grew by 200,000 jobs or fewer, in which the unemployment rate fell to 5.3 percent but not to 5.2 percent, and in which average hourly earnings rose just modestly could convince market participants that the Fed would refrain from raising interest rates later this month, they said.

"There's risk in the unemployment rate," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc. "It could instantaneously become the major factor tomorrow if it drops to 5.2 percent."

Karydakis said the market expects the unemployment rate to return to its six-month trend of 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent in January. "The risk is that it will decline more than that and that would not sit well with the market," said Karydakis. "5.3 percent people should be able to handle. 5.2 percent will be a problem. It would reignite the worst fears of the market about an economy that does not seem to be slowing down."
Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said the unemployment rate and the average hourly earnings figure could attract special attention.
"They could be more significant than the headline payrolls number," he said.
Still, a contingent of market analysts were not persuaded that solid February employment growth would necessarily lead the Federal Reserve to tighten interest rates late this month.

"Our forecast for payroll growth of 220,000 jobs, a longer workweek and a 0.4 percent or 0.5 percent rise in average hourly earnings would be neutral for Fed policy," said Peter D'Antonio, senior economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A.
"You can't rule out that they would move pre-emptively, but I think the odds are against that," he said.
James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc., agreed.

"As strong as the economic news is, the inflation news is just as surprising," he said. "Inflation is stable. The inflation news for the next few months is going to make it very difficult for the Fed to make a case that inflation is accelerating."
The market will also get January consumer installment credit data from the Fed at 1500 EST/2000 GMT on Friday. Those data are not expected to affect the market.
"Clearly, the pace of consumer credit accumulation has been slowing, which is a positive development which raises the prospect of a sustainably healthy consumer," said Karydakis.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-1/8 percent and 5-3/16 percent on Friday.
